messages.subject: About occuComm function
messages.body_plain:
Dear Ken and colleagues,
Thank you very much for the updated unmarked package and the improvements to the occuComm function, it looks very interesting.

I was wondering whether it would be possible to apply that function to a larger study area (multi-regions), for example across different study regions of the country. Because I am thinking of using that function by including different study regions as a random effect in my model.

Thanks in advance for your help and I would greatly appreciate any guidance you can provide on this.

Best regards,
Lwin

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] About occuComm function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Lwin,

You can include a random intercept in the occuComm formula. However I think it would be better to have both random intercepts *and slopes* by region. Unfortunately occuComm does currently support random slopes for grouping factors besides species. For that you'd have to code a custom model in JAGS or nimble, or fit separate models by region.

Ken

messages.subject: Distance sampling in unmarked: Violations of detection ~ distance assumption for some bird species
messages.subject_clean: Distance sampling in unmarked: Violations of detection ~ distance assumption for some bird species
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm working with transects data for birds and fitting distance sampling models using the gdistsamp function in the unmarked R package. My distance bins are: 0–25 m, 25–100 m and 100–1000 m (as the surveys are done following these bins too).

For most species, things behave as expected — higher counts in closer bins and fewer at longer distances. But for a few species, I’m observing the opposite: most detections are in the farthest bin (100–1000 m), and very few in the closest one. This seems to violate the assumption that detection probability declines with distance, which is fundamental to distance sampling. Probably, these happen due to issues with species-specific detectability (e.g., loud calls detectable far away).

My questions are:

What are the best practices in this case — is it valid to fit distance sampling models at all for these species?

Is there any workaround in unmarked::gdistsamp to handle this violation (e.g., alternate key functions, model truncation, or bin adjustments)?

Would you recommend switching to a different model type for these species?

Could this reflect a problem with the distance bins themselves (e.g., too wide/few)?

I’d appreciate any advice or references on handling this kind of issue. Thanks in advance!

Best,

Gabri

hi Gabri,
 From what I understand here, your 3rd distance bin spans 100 m - 1000m and as such is much wider than the other two. Therefore you might expect more detections in that bin simply because the expected number of birds in that bin is 9x the other two bins combined.  Therefore I don't think you have a problem here.
regards
andy

messages.body_plain:
Dear Gaby,

I think your data may still adhere to the model's assumptions, since your final bin is extremely wide. If p is not very small, then I think it's possible to have more detections in that bin than closer-by. I think you should make a parametric bootstrap GoF to test this assumption, rather than just visually checking the raw data.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Capture-recapture workshop in Mallorca/Spain, 24-28 Nov 2025
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

Giacomo Tavecchia and his group at the IMEDEA in Esporles/Spain are offering a capture-recapture workshop this fall. This is in beautiful Mallorca (for Americans: this is something like Cancun) so hurry up to sign up to the course. Information here below.

Best regards  --- Marc

We are planning an introductory course on capture-mark-recapture and -recovery (CMRR) analyses, to be held in Mallorca (Spain), 24–28 November 2025.

 The course is designed for students, researchers, and environmental managers interested in learning the fundamentals of this evolving field. No prior knowledge of CMRR methods is required.

 At this stage, we are opening a pre-inscription to assess interest and finalize logistics.

👉 If you’re interested, please send a short message to  g.tav...@uib.es with your name, background, and intention to attend (non-binding).

📌 More details:  https://animaldemography.blogspot.com/p/workshop.html

 We’ll get back to all pre-registered participants once official registration opens.

Thank you

Giacomo Tavecchia

messages.subject: do pcount models with random effects still require specifying engine = "TMB"?
messages.subject_clean: do pcount models with random effects still require specifying engine = "TMB"?
messages.body_plain: I'm running hiearhical, repeated-counts, N-mixture models using the pcount function in package unmarked. All my models include a random effect of region in the detection model, but I did not specify which engine to use. I just noticed that in the documentation, it says the pcount function "requires" specifying the TMB engine to run random effects. To test that, I re-ran my best-supported model specifying engine="TMB", but there was no difference in the model results or parameter estimates. The documentation for the occu function states that "TMB is used automatically if the model formula contains random effects". Is that now also the case with the pcount function, or do I need to re-run all my  models and specify engine="TMB"?

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] do pcount models with random effects still require specifying engine = "TMB"?
messages.body_plain:
If you specify a random effect, then TMB should automatically be used. You can check this by just looking at the model output - if you specified a random effect you should see the random effect estimates in the summary.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm building a colext model with the same predictor terms on psi, col and ext. These terms are constant over the entire survey period. When I run the VIF command on each submodel, I get acceptable values for the psi submodel but high VIFs for the same terms in the col and ext submodels. Is this expected, given that the values of each variable are the same year-on-year?

Thanks in advance,
Rory

messages.subject: Predict impact of covariates on community using occuComm
messages.subject_clean: Predict impact of covariates on community using occuComm
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am running occuComm models in R to study about community ecology in tropical forest in India. I have created a few hypotheses and have divided different species into different communities based on their size, diet, and tolerance to human.

Let's say I have one hypothesis under which there is a community made up of tiger, leopard, and dhole.

Now I run my models and have a most-supported model.

Is there a way to predict the impact of the covariates used in this model on the community rather than separately for each species in the community?

Any help would be really appreciated.

Thanks,
Sprih

Hi Sprih,

If you use the predict function on the model with the argument re.form = NA, that will give you predictions for the community-level average effect.

Ken
